cultivar: Fuding Dabai (typical of the shou mei base)
processing: Coarse white tea, usually shou mei, is piled, steamed, pressed and then held in conditions that grow the golden fungus Eurotium cristatum, the step borrowed from Fu brick dark tea, before final drying.
harvest_season: The base is shou mei, a late and mature picking; the fungal flowering happens later, during brick making, so the harvest season matters less than the base tea and the flowering.
appearance_dry: A dark olive-brown brick of coarse leaf, flecked inside with tiny golden-yellow specks.
appearance_wet: Coarse brown-olive leaves and stems, softened and broken from pressing.
taste_profile: Sweet and mellow, with a sweet fruity aroma; comparative work finds the cup redder and gentler than ordinary Fu brick.

brewing.notes: Pry the brick gently so the golden specks stay in the leaf. Water just off the boil suits it, and the spent leaves can be simmered as with other coarse aged teas.

vintage_note: A new product style, sold by pressing batch and year rather than as a seasonal fresh tea. As with Fu bricks, a lot is ready to drink once flowered; extra keeping is optional, and dry, odour-free storage matters.
description:
This is a hybrid: white tea leaf with dark tea craft. Shou mei from Fujian takes the place of the usual dark tea base, and it is pressed and flowered the way Fu brick is, so the golden specks of Eurotium cristatum grow through it.

The piling, steaming and flowering change the leaf a great deal. Measured in processing studies, tea polyphenols, catechins and amino acids fall as theabrownin and flavonoids rise, so it drinks far from a fresh white tea. That is why it can feel closer to a brick than to the shou mei it began as.

Expect a redder liquor and a sweet, fruity, mellow cup, softer than a Fu brick. Use hot water and short early steeps, then let it run longer as the pressed leaf loosens.

The finishing work is not tied to any one place: sellers name Fuding leaf, and Fu brick craft traces to Jingyang in Shaanxi. Ask where the leaf came from and where the brick was flowered. The golden specks should be real fungal bodies, evenly spread, and the brick should smell clean rather than musty.
history: This is a recent style with no long documented history. Its background is Fu brick, a dark tea whose flowering method is closely associated with Jingyang in Shaanxi. Producers and food scientists have since applied that step to Fujian shou mei, and studies now examine golden flower white tea as its own product.
